title: Part 1, Chapter 1
paragraphs: About the character and pursuits of the famous gentleman Don Quixote of La Mancha

In a village in La Mancha — the name of which I'd rather not recall — there lived not long ago one of those gentlemen who keep a lance in the rack, an old shield, a lean hack, and a greyhound for hunting. A stew of rather more beef than mutton, a salad most nights, leftovers on Saturdays, lentils on Fridays, and an extra pigeon on Sundays ate up three-quarters of his income. The rest went on a fine wool doublet, velvet breeches with matching shoes for holidays, and his best homespun for weekdays, in which he cut a respectable figure. His household included a housekeeper past forty, a niece under twenty, and a lad who could both saddle the horse and handle the pruning-hook out in the fields and at market. Our gentleman was nearly fifty; he was lean, sinewy, sharp-featured, an early riser and a great hunter. They say his surname was Quixada — or Quesada; the authorities differ — though reasonable inference suggests he was actually called Quexana. This is of little importance to the story; it's enough that the telling not stray a hair's breadth from the truth.

You should know, then, that this gentleman, whenever he had time on his hands (which was most of the year), gave himself over to reading chivalric romances with such enthusiasm and addiction that he almost entirely neglected his hunting and even the management of his property. His mania reached the point where he sold off acres of tilled land to buy more romances, and he brought home every one he could lay hands on. Of all of them, none pleased him more than the work of the famous Feliciano de Silva, whose clarity of style and tangled conceits struck him as pearls beyond price — especially when he came upon the courtship scenes and challenges, where he routinely found passages like "_the reason of the unreason with which my reason is afflicted so weakens my reason that with reason I murmur at your beauty;_" or again, "_the high heavens, that of your divinity divinely fortify you with the stars, render you deserving of the desert your greatness deserves_." Over conceits of that kind the poor gentleman lost his mind, lying awake trying to unpick them and force the meaning out — meaning that Aristotle himself, brought back to life for the purpose, could not have extracted. He was not at all easy about the wounds that Don Belianis gave and took, because however great the surgeons who patched him up, he had to be scarred and seamed from head to toe. But he approved of how the author ended his book with the promise of that interminable adventure, and was many a time tempted to pick up his pen and finish it himself along the lines the text suggests — which he no doubt would have done, and done well, if greater and more absorbing thoughts had not kept getting in the way.

He had many an argument with the village priest (a learned man, a Sigüenza graduate) over which had been the greater knight, Palmerin of England or Amadis of Gaul. Master Nicholas, the village barber, would maintain that neither could touch the Knight of Phoebus, and that if anyone could compare with _him_, it was Don Galaor, Amadis's brother — because Galaor had a spirit equal to any occasion, was no fussy or weepy knight like Amadis, and lost nothing to him in raw valour. In short, our gentleman became so absorbed in his books that he was reading from sunset to sunrise and from dawn till dark, and what with little sleep and constant reading his brain dried out and he lost his wits altogether. His head filled up with what he had been reading — enchantments, quarrels, battles, challenges, wounds, courtships, loves, agonies, and every variety of impossible nonsense — and the whole fabric of invention he had read of took on the weight of truth in his mind, so that to him no history in the world was more real. He used to say that the Cid Ruy Diaz was a very fine knight, but no match for the Knight of the Burning Sword, who with a single backstroke cut two ferocious giants in half. He thought even better of Bernardo del Carpio because at Roncesvalles he killed the enchanted Roland, using Hercules's trick of strangling Antaeus, son of Earth, in his arms. He had great respect for the giant Morgante because, although of the giant breed (which is always arrogant and badly behaved), Morgante alone was affable and well brought up. But above all he admired Reinaldos of Montalbán, especially when Reinaldos rode out from his castle and robbed everyone he met, and when, overseas, he stole that image of Mohammed that the history says was solid gold. For a chance to kick the traitor Ganelon around, he would have handed over his housekeeper, and his niece into the bargain.

In short, his wits being completely gone, he hit upon the strangest notion any madman ever hit upon: that it was both right and necessary — both for his own honour and the service of his country — to turn himself into a knight-errant, ride out into the world in full armour in search of adventures, and put into practice everything he had read of as the standard business of knights-errant — righting every kind of wrong, exposing himself to dangers from which, in the end, he would earn undying fame and renown. The poor man already saw himself crowned at the very least Emperor of Trebizond by the might of his arm; and so, carried away by the sheer pleasure of these fancies, he set about putting his plan into action immediately.

The first thing he did was clean up some armour that had belonged to his great-grandfather and had been lying forgotten in a corner for generations, eaten with rust and covered with mildew. He scoured and polished it as best he could, but he could see one major defect: it had no closed helmet, only a simple morion. He compensated with ingenuity, contriving a kind of half-helmet out of pasteboard that, fitted over the morion, looked like the real thing. True, when he drew his sword to test whether it would stand a cut, the first slash undid in an instant what had taken him a week to make. The ease with which he had reduced it to pieces left him uneasy, so to be safe he rebuilt it, this time fixing iron strips on the inside until he was satisfied with its strength; and then, not caring to run any more experiments, he accepted it as a helmet of the most perfect construction.

He next turned to inspect his horse, which — with more cracks in its hooves than a worn-out coin and more blemishes than Gonela's old nag, _tantum pellis et ossa fuit_ — in his eyes surpassed Alexander's Bucephalus or the Cid's Babieca. Four days were spent thinking up a name, on the grounds (as he said to himself) that it would not be right for a horse belonging to so famous a knight, with such merits of his own, to go without a distinguished name; and he wanted the name to indicate both what the horse had been before he belonged to a knight-errant and what he was now, since it was only fair that, the master taking a new role, the horse take a new name to match — something lofty and full-sounding, suited to the new order and calling he was about to follow. So after composing, crossing out, rejecting, adding to, unmaking, and remaking a great many names out of his memory and imagination, he settled on calling him Rocinante: a name, to his ear, lofty, sonorous, and significant of the horse's condition as a previous hack and his present standing as the first and foremost of all the hacks in the world.

Having found a name for his horse that pleased him, he wanted one for himself, and he spent eight more days on the question, finally settling on "Don Quixote" — from which, as has been mentioned, the authors of this truthful history have inferred that his name must beyond doubt have been Quixada, and not Quesada as some claim. Recalling, though, that the valiant Amadis was not satisfied to be called simply Amadis but added the name of his kingdom and country to make it famous — Amadis of Gaul — he likewise resolved, as a good knight, to attach his own region's name to his own, and to style himself Don Quixote of La Mancha. That, he reckoned, gave an accurate account of his origin and country and did honour to it by taking his surname from it.

So, with his armour polished, his morion converted into a helmet, his horse christened, and himself confirmed, he concluded that nothing further was needed except to find a lady to be in love with; for a knight-errant without love was like a tree without leaves or fruit, or a body without a soul. He said to himself, "If, for my sins — or by my good fortune — I come across some giant out here, which is a normal thing for knights-errant, and unhorse him at the first charge, or split him in two at the waist, or in short defeat and subdue him, won't it be useful to have someone to send him to as a gift, so that he may come in and fall on his knees before my sweet lady and say, in a humble, submissive voice, 'I am the giant Caraculiambro, lord of the island of Malindrania, vanquished in single combat by the never sufficiently praised knight Don Quixote of La Mancha, who has commanded me to present myself before Your Grace, that your Highness may dispose of me at your pleasure'?" Oh, how our gentleman enjoyed this little speech, especially when he had thought of someone to name as his Lady! There was, the story says, in a village near his own, a very good-looking farm girl whom he had once been in love with — though, as far as anyone knows, she never noticed and certainly never gave it a thought. Her name was Aldonza Lorenzo, and he decided to promote her to Lady of his Thoughts. After hunting for a name in keeping with hers, one that would suggest a princess and great lady, he settled on Dulcinea del Toboso (she being from El Toboso): a name, to his mind, musical, uncommon, and significant, like all the others he had already bestowed on himself and on the things belonging to him.
